groups.name: Hygiene
groups.desc: Seven of Ambit's eleven forensic-accounting ratios that our data can support. Used as a quality gate, not as an archetype.
groups.plain: A health check on the accounting, not a measure of how good the business is. It asks whether reported profit looks like real, steady, cash-backed profit.
groups.read: The score (0-100) is the average percentile of seven accounting ratios, so 50 is average and higher is cleaner. The decile turns it into 1 (cleanest tenth of companies) to 10 (least clean). Deciles 8-10 are Ambit's 'zone of darkness'. It flags companies to read carefully; it does not prove anything is wrong.

groups.name: Customers fund the business
groups.desc: Advances and negative working capital: customers (not lenders or shareholders) finance operations.
groups.plain: Companies where customers, not lenders or shareholders, fund the working capital: they pay upfront, so the company can grow without tying up its own money.
groups.read: The score (0-100) averages the percentile rank of six metrics. 50 is typical, 75 or more is strong, 90 or more is very strong. It is blank when too few of the metrics could be computed (for example a company with no trade payables line). Real estate, defence and capital goods score high by nature, so compare like with like.

groups.name: Stickiness
groups.desc: Customers keep coming back: steady sales, steady margins, steady collections. Numbers show consistency, not stickiness itself.
groups.plain: Companies whose business keeps coming back: sales rarely fall, margins and collections stay steady. This shows consistency; it cannot show why customers stay.
groups.read: The score (0-100) averages the percentile rank of six steadiness metrics. A high score means steady, not necessarily growing. Confirm the reason (repeat orders, switching costs, contracts) in the concalls and annual reports.

groups.name: Bargaining power
groups.desc: Margins held or widened, including in years the universe's margins fell, while growing and collecting on time.
groups.plain: Companies that hold or widen their margins, including when costs rose for everyone, while still growing and getting paid on time. The footprint of being able to pass costs on.
groups.read: The score (0-100) averages the percentile rank of five metrics. High means margins behaved better than typical. The data cannot separate price rises from lower costs; concall commentary on realisation versus volume does.

groups.name: Resilience
groups.desc: Held up better than the universe in its worst years; shallow drawdowns, quick recoveries, no losses.
groups.plain: Companies that held up better than the rest in the universe's worst years, and recovered quicker from their own bad patches.
groups.read: The score (0-100) averages the percentile rank of seven metrics. High means shallow drawdowns, no losses, positive cash flow and better-than-typical performance in stress years. The stress years are chosen from the data and listed in the Method tab.

groups.name: Self-funded compounding
groups.desc: High incremental returns on capital without leaning on debt. Reinvestment, sustainable growth and dilution are shown but not scored.
groups.plain: Companies that earn high returns on the new capital they put to work and do it without leaning on debt.
groups.read: The score (0-100) averages the percentile rank of two scored metrics (incremental ROCE and debt to equity); the other three are shown for context only. Treat it as a first filter, not a conclusion.

groups.name: Cost leadership
groups.desc: Higher margins and asset turns with lean working capital. Until industry labels exist these are universe and size-bucket comparisons, not peer comparisons.
groups.plain: Companies that make more operating profit from each rupee of sales and of assets, and keep inventory and receivables lean.
groups.read: The score (0-100) averages the percentile rank of six metrics. Margins and asset use differ hugely between industries, and industry labels do not exist yet, so for now this partly rewards high-margin sectors. A true cost leader beats its own industry's median.

metrics.name: Cumulative CFO / EBITDA
metrics.desc: Do profits turn into operating cash over the whole window? Low suggests aggressive revenue recognition or working-capital build (Ambit #1).
metrics.plain: Over the whole period, how many rupees of operating cash the business actually collected for every rupee of operating profit (EBITDA) it reported.
metrics.read: Higher is better. Around 1.0 means profits turn into cash. Under about 0.6 means profit is stuck in receivables or inventory, or is booked aggressively. A fast-growing company can be low for an honest reason, so check working capital before judging.

metrics.name: Depreciation-rate volatility
metrics.desc: Median absolute year-on-year change in depreciation / opening net block (Ambit #2; net block stands in for gross block).
metrics.plain: How much the yearly depreciation charge, as a share of the asset base, jumps around from one year to the next.
metrics.read: Lower is better. Depreciation should be steady when the asset base is steady. A value of 1% means the rate typically moves one percentage point a year. Big swings can mean accounting policy changes that flatter profit, but mergers and big capex also cause jumps, so it is a prompt to look, not proof.

metrics.name: Other-income volatility
metrics.desc: Median absolute year-on-year change in other income as a share of sales (Ambit #3).
metrics.plain: How much 'other income' (interest, gains on selling assets, one-offs) swings as a share of sales.
metrics.read: Lower is better. Some companies book one-off gains in weak years to prop up profit. A small, steady figure is clean. A large swing deserves a look at what the other income actually was.

metrics.name: Cash yield
metrics.desc: Other income / opening cash and investments, median (Ambit #5). Low means idle or misreported cash; other income also holds non-treasury items.
metrics.plain: Other income divided by the cash and investments held at the start of the year: roughly the return the company earns on its cash pile.
metrics.read: Higher is better, up to a point. Cash should earn about the going interest rate, say 5-8%. Very low can mean the cash is smaller than reported, trapped, or idle. Very high usually means other income holds gains or non-cash items, and companies with almost no cash show silly ratios.

metrics.name: Reserves growth vs retained profit
metrics.desc: Change in reserves / (profit - dividends), median (Ambit #6). Below 1 can mean direct write-offs through equity.
metrics.plain: How much the company's reserves grew compared with the profit it kept after paying dividends.
metrics.read: Scored higher-is-better, but the healthy value is close to 1. A value near 1 means retained profit became reserves. Clearly below 1 can mean losses or write-offs went straight to equity instead of through the profit and loss account. Above 1 can come from share premium, revaluations or acquisitions. Only measured in years with retained profit.

metrics.name: CWIP / fixed assets (25th pct)
metrics.desc: Persistently high capital work in progress can mean unsubstantiated or delayed capex (Ambit #9; 25th percentile as in the paper).
metrics.plain: How much of the fixed assets are still 'under construction' (capital work in progress), using the 25th-percentile year so one big project year does not dominate.
metrics.read: Lower is better. A persistently high share means projects are slow to finish, or spending is not turning into working assets. Companies in the middle of building a plant are legitimately high for a few years.

metrics.name: Cum (CFO+CFI) / median sales
metrics.desc: Cash left after investing, over a typical year's sales (Ambit #10).
metrics.plain: The cash left after running the business and investing in it, added up across the period, compared with one typical year of sales.
metrics.read: Higher is better. Positive means the business funds its own growth. Strongly negative means it kept needing outside money. A value of 0.1 means that over the whole period it kept cash worth 10% of a year's sales. Buying financial investments counts as investing, so acquisitive or investment-heavy companies look worse.

metrics.name: Advance days
metrics.desc: Customer advances / sales x 365, median of the last 5 years.
metrics.plain: How many days of sales the company is holding as advances from customers: money received before the goods or services are delivered.
metrics.read: Higher is better for the customers-fund-the-business idea. 0 means no advances; 10 means customers have prepaid about ten days of sales. Real estate, defence and capital goods always take advances, so compare within a business type. If it is collapsing, orders may be drying up.

metrics.name: Advance momentum
metrics.desc: 5-year CAGR of advances minus 5-year CAGR of sales. Positive means orders are queuing up faster than sales.
metrics.plain: Whether advances from customers have grown faster than sales over five years.
metrics.read: Higher is better. Positive means more customers are paying upfront relative to sales: orders are queuing up. Negative means advances have shrunk relative to sales. Blank when the company had no advances at either end of the five years.

metrics.name: Advance share of funding
metrics.desc: Advances / (advances + trade payables): separates customer funding from supplier credit.
metrics.plain: Advances as a share of advances plus trade payables: who finances the company's day-to-day float, customers or suppliers.
metrics.read: Higher means customers, rather than suppliers, provide more of the float. 0 means all supplier credit; 0.5 means half and half. Customer money is usually the stronger signal, because prepaying shows demand, while supplier credit can just reflect stretched bills.

metrics.name: Trade working capital % sales
metrics.desc: (Receivables + inventory - trade payables - advances) / sales, last 5 years. More negative is better.
metrics.plain: Money tied up in operating working capital as a percentage of sales: receivables plus inventory, minus what is owed to suppliers, minus customer advances.
metrics.read: Lower is better, and negative is the prize. Negative means customers and suppliers fund the business, so growth releases cash. 20% means ₹20 sits in working capital for every ₹100 of sales. Retail and FMCG run low, engineering and exports run high. A negative number driven by unpaid supplier bills rather than advances is a warning, so check the advance share (C3).

metrics.name: Incremental working capital
metrics.desc: Change in trade working capital / change in sales over 5 years. Negative means growth releases cash.
metrics.plain: For each extra rupee of sales added over five years, how many extra rupees had to be tied up in working capital.
metrics.read: Lower is better. Negative means growth released cash. 0.2 means every ₹1 of extra sales needed ₹0.20 of extra working capital. Only calculated when sales grew over the five years.

metrics.name: Working-capital trend
metrics.desc: Recent half of the window minus the earlier half (median trade working capital % sales). Falling is better.
metrics.plain: Whether working capital as a share of sales is getting better or worse: the recent years against the earlier years.
metrics.read: Lower (more negative) is better. Negative means the business needs less working capital than it used to. Positive means customers are paying slower or inventory is building up.

metrics.name: Years sales fell
metrics.desc: Number of years with negative sales growth.
metrics.plain: How many of the years in the window had lower sales than the year before.
metrics.read: Lower is better. 0 means sales never fell. Three or more in ten is common for cyclical and small companies. Look at when the falls happened: one dip in the COVID year is different from steady shrinking.

metrics.name: Worst sales growth
metrics.desc: The single worst year-on-year sales growth in the window.
metrics.plain: The worst single year of sales growth, in other words the biggest fall.
metrics.read: Higher is better. -5% means the worst year was a 5% fall; -40% means sales collapsed at some point. A positive number means sales grew every year.

metrics.name: Growth consistency
metrics.desc: Sales CAGR / standard deviation of annual growth: how much growth per unit of bumpiness.
metrics.plain: Sales growth per unit of bumpiness: the long-run growth rate divided by how much the yearly growth rate swings.
metrics.read: Higher is better. About 1 means the growth rate roughly equals its swings. Above 2 is steady compounding. Below 0.3 is lumpy or erratic growth. Needs at least four years of growth figures.

metrics.name: Operating-margin volatility
metrics.desc: Median absolute year-on-year change in operating margin.
metrics.plain: How much the operating margin typically moves from one year to the next.
metrics.read: Lower is better. 1% means the margin usually moves about one percentage point a year. Very steady margins suggest stable pricing and costs. Compare within a business type: commodity businesses swing more.

metrics.name: Receivable-days volatility
metrics.desc: Median absolute year-on-year change in receivable days: customers paying on a steady rhythm.
metrics.plain: How much the number of days customers take to pay changes from year to year.
metrics.read: Lower is better, measured in days. A steady rhythm suggests customers behave consistently. Big swings suggest changing credit terms or collection trouble.

metrics.name: Quarterly sales-growth dispersion
metrics.desc: Standard deviation of year-on-year growth across the latest quarters (needs 4+ comparable quarters).
metrics.plain: How much year-on-year growth varies across the latest quarters.
metrics.read: Lower is better. 5% means quarterly growth rates differ from their average by about five percentage points; above about 20% is very lumpy. Uses only the last ten or so quarters Screener provides, and needs at least four comparable quarters.

metrics.name: Margin expansion
metrics.desc: Median operating margin of the recent half of the window minus the earlier half.
metrics.plain: The typical operating margin in the later years minus the typical margin in the earlier years.
metrics.read: Higher is better. +2% means margins are two percentage points higher than they used to be. Read it together with growth: widening margin while growing is the footprint of pricing power. A fall can be industry-wide, not the company's fault.

metrics.name: Margin in cost-shock years
metrics.desc: In the years the universe's median margin fell most, the company's margin change minus the universe median change. Positive means it held up better.
metrics.plain: In the years when most companies' margins fell the most, how this company's margin change compares with the typical company's.
metrics.read: Higher is better. 0 means it moved like the typical company; +2% means it held up two points better; negative means it was hit harder. The years are chosen from the data and listed in the Method tab. Blank if the company lacks data for those years.

metrics.name: Margin-accretive growth years
metrics.desc: Share of years with sales growth above the universe median and no margin loss.
metrics.plain: The share of years in which the company grew faster than the typical company and did not lose any margin.
metrics.read: Higher is better. 50% means half the years it out-grew the typical company without giving up margin. It is hard to do: most companies manage it in under a third of years.

metrics.name: Receivable-days trend
metrics.desc: Recent minus earlier median receivable days. Rising while pushing price is a warning.
metrics.plain: Whether customers now take longer or shorter to pay than they did earlier in the period.
metrics.read: Lower (more negative) is better. +20 days means customers now take twenty days longer. Rising days while pushing prices or growth can mean sales are being bought with credit.

metrics.name: Years ROCE above 15%
metrics.desc: Share of years with (PBT + interest) / (equity + reserves + borrowings) above 15%.
metrics.plain: The share of years the company earned more than 15% on its capital (profit before tax plus interest, over equity plus reserves plus borrowings).
metrics.read: Higher is better. 100% means every year; 20% means two years in ten. 15% is a rough hurdle above typical borrowing costs. It uses year-end capital. Capital-light businesses score high by nature.

metrics.name: Sales growth in stress years
metrics.desc: In the years the universe's median sales growth was lowest, the company's growth minus the universe median.
metrics.plain: In the years the whole universe's sales growth was weakest, how much faster or slower this company grew than the typical company.
metrics.read: Higher is better. +10% means it grew ten points faster than typical in the bad years; negative means it was hit harder. The bad years are chosen from the data and listed in the Method tab.

metrics.name: Operating-profit drawdown
metrics.desc: Largest peak-to-trough fall in operating profit within the window.
metrics.plain: The biggest fall in operating profit from an earlier peak to a later low.
metrics.read: Lower is better. 30% means operating profit fell 30% from its peak at worst. Above 100% means operating profit turned negative. Cyclical businesses naturally show large drawdowns.

metrics.name: Years to recover
metrics.desc: Years from the trough back to the prior operating-profit peak (0 if the drawdown was under 5%; counted to the end of the window if not yet recovered).
metrics.plain: How many years it took operating profit to climb back to its earlier peak after its worst fall.
metrics.read: Lower is better. 0 means no meaningful fall (under 5%). If profit has not yet recovered, it counts the years to the end of the window, so a high number can simply mean 'still down'.

metrics.name: Loss years
metrics.desc: Number of years with negative net profit.
metrics.plain: The number of years the company reported a net loss.
metrics.read: Lower is better. 0 is best. One or two in ten can be a one-off bad patch; more than that suggests fragility.

metrics.name: Years with positive CFO
metrics.desc: Share of years with positive operating cash flow.
metrics.plain: The share of years in which the business generated positive cash from its operations.
metrics.read: Higher is better. 100% means operating cash flow was positive every year. Under about 70% means the business often consumed cash.

metrics.name: Minimum interest cover
metrics.desc: Lowest (operating profit - depreciation) / interest in the window; capped at 100 and treated as 100 if the company has no interest at all.
metrics.plain: In its worst year, how many times operating profit (after depreciation) covered the interest bill.
metrics.read: Higher is better. Above 3 is comfortable; below 1.5 is tight; negative means operating profit did not even cover depreciation. Capped at 100, and companies with no interest cost at all show 100.

metrics.name: Share price in stress years
metrics.desc: Year-end price change in the years the universe's median price change was lowest, minus that median. Market-based and annual only; do not combine with price backtests.
metrics.plain: How the share price did in the years the whole universe's median price fell most, compared with the typical company.
metrics.read: Higher is better. +10% means it fell ten points less (or rose ten points more) than typical. Based on year-end prices only, so it is crude. It is market-based, so do not use it together with a price-return backtest.

metrics.name: Incremental ROCE
metrics.desc: Change in (PBT + interest) / change in capital employed over 5 years, when capital grew.
metrics.plain: For each extra rupee of capital the business added over five years, how many extra rupees of annual profit (before tax and interest) it earned.
metrics.read: Higher is better. 20% means the new capital earns 20% a year. If it is above the company's existing return, new money is working at least as hard as old money. Only calculated when capital grew.

metrics.name: Debt / equity
metrics.desc: Borrowings / (share capital + reserves), median.
metrics.plain: Borrowings compared with shareholders' money (share capital plus reserves).
metrics.read: Lower is better here. 0.5 means ₹50 of debt for every ₹100 of equity; 0 means debt-free. Banks and finance companies run very high ratios by design.

metrics.name: Reinvestment rate
metrics.desc: Capex proxy / operating cash flow, median. Shown, not scored: more reinvestment is only good if returns hold.
metrics.plain: How much of the cash from operations was put back into fixed assets.
metrics.read: Shown but not scored. 60% means 60 paise of each ₹1 of operating cash went into capex. High reinvestment is good only if returns hold up (see incremental ROCE); otherwise it is just spending.

metrics.name: Growth minus sustainable growth
metrics.desc: 5-year sales CAGR minus median (ROE x retention). Positive means growth needs outside funding. Shown, not scored.
metrics.plain: How much faster sales grew than the company could fund from its own retained profit (return on equity times the share of profit kept).
metrics.read: Shown but not scored. Positive means growth needed outside funding such as debt, new equity, or supplier and customer money. Negative means the company grew slower than it could fund itself.

metrics.name: Share-count CAGR
metrics.desc: 5-year CAGR of shares outstanding. Shown, not scored: splits and bonuses distort it.
metrics.plain: How fast the number of shares in issue has grown per year over five years.
metrics.read: Shown but not scored. 0 means no new shares. Splits and bonus issues also raise the count without diluting anyone, so check before reading it as dilution.

metrics.name: Operating margin (median)
metrics.desc: Median operating margin. Rank against industry peers once classification exists.
metrics.plain: The company's typical operating margin: operating profit as a share of sales.
metrics.read: Higher is better. 15% means ₹15 of operating profit for every ₹100 of sales. Margins differ hugely by business, so it only means something against similar companies. Until industry labels exist, a high value may simply mean a high-margin sector.

metrics.name: Asset turnover
metrics.desc: Sales / (net block + CWIP), median.
metrics.plain: Sales generated for each rupee of fixed assets (net block plus capital work in progress).
metrics.read: Higher is better. 3 means ₹3 of sales for each ₹1 of fixed assets. Asset-light businesses are high by nature. A high turnover with a high margin is the mark of an efficient operator.

metrics.name: Operating profit / fixed assets
metrics.desc: Operating profit per rupee of net block plus CWIP, median.
metrics.plain: Operating profit earned for each rupee of fixed assets.
metrics.read: Higher is better. 0.3 means 30 paise of annual operating profit per ₹1 of fixed assets. It blends margin and asset use into one number.

metrics.name: Sales CAGR (5y)
metrics.desc: Growth proxy for share gain; compare with the industry median once classification exists.
metrics.plain: How fast sales have grown per year over the last five years.
metrics.read: Higher is better. It stands in for winning customers or share, but until industry labels exist we cannot say whether it beats the company's own industry. Needs positive sales at both ends.

metrics.name: Inventory days
metrics.desc: Inventory / sales x 365, last 5 years (sales-based, no cost-of-goods in the data).
metrics.plain: How many days of sales the company holds as inventory.
metrics.read: Lower is better. 60 means about two months of sales sitting in stock. It uses sales, not cost of goods, as the base, so it overstates for low-margin businesses. Retail and FMCG run low; capital goods and jewellery run high.

metrics.name: Receivable days
metrics.desc: Receivables / sales x 365, last 5 years.
metrics.plain: How many days of sales are still waiting to be collected from customers.
metrics.read: Lower is better. 60 means about two months of sales are uncollected. Exporters, government suppliers and project businesses run higher. A rising number means slower collections.
